cards.objective: Identify the sphenoid bone on the skull.

why.t: It is the single, complex bone in the centre of the skull base, and it reaches out to the sides of the skull. It is called the keystone bone because it joins with almost every other bone of the skull.

simpler.t: It sits in the middle of the floor of the skull and touches almost every other skull bone, like the keystone of an arch.

depth.t: Lesser wings: the ridge between the anterior and middle cranial fossae.
Sella turcica: in the midline; its hypophyseal fossa holds the pituitary gland.
Greater wings: the anterior floor of the middle cranial fossa and part of the side of the skull.
Its body contains the sphenoid sinus, the most posterior paranasal sinus.
Its greater wing is one of the four bones that meet at the pterion.

clinical.t: Because the sphenoid sinus lies just in front of and below the sella turcica, surgeons can reach a pituitary tumour through the nose and the sphenoid sinus (transsphenoidal surgery), without opening the skull.
clinical.check: Transsphenoidal surgery is not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–9, 12–16, 20); the sinus position is.

hook.t: “Sphenoid” comes from the Greek for wedge: it is wedged between the other bones of the skull.
hook.check: Etymology (Greek sphēn, wedge) is not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–9, 12–16, 20).

trap.t: Do not confuse it with the ethmoid, the smaller midline bone in front of it whose cribriform plates form the roof of the nasal cavity.

cards.objective: State which bone contains the foramen magnum.
cards.front: Which bone contains the foramen magnum?

why.t: The occipital bone forms the back of the skull and the back of its base. The foramen magnum opens in that base so that the spinal cord can leave the skull.

simpler.t: The bone at the back of the head has a big hole underneath, and the spinal cord passes through it.

depth.t: Lies in the midline of the posterior cranial fossa, the deepest of the three fossae.
The posterior cranial fossa holds the cerebellum.
Occipital condyles on either side form joints with the first cervical vertebra.
The hypoglossal canals open at its anterolateral margin, carrying the nerve to the tongue.

clinical.t: Raised pressure inside the skull can push the lowest part of the cerebellum (the tonsils) down through the foramen magnum, compressing the brainstem: “coning”, which can stop breathing.
clinical.check: Tonsillar herniation is not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–9, 12–16, 20).

trap.t: The foramen magnum is in the occipital bone, not the temporal bone: the temporal bone’s opening beside the posterior fossa is the internal acoustic meatus.

cards.objective: Name the artery that lies deep to the pterion.
cards.front: Which artery lies immediately deep to the pterion?

why.t: The pterion is where four skull bones meet, and it is the weakest part of the skull. A major branch of the artery that supplies the skull and the coverings of the brain runs on its inner surface, so a blow here can fracture the bone and tear the artery.
why.check: OpenStax does not name the artery; “middle meningeal” needs an approved source.

simpler.t: The pterion is a thin spot on the side of the head. An important artery runs just inside it, so a hard knock there can break the bone and the artery.

depth.t: Four bones meet in an H-shaped suture: frontal, parietal, temporal (squamous part) and sphenoid (greater wing).
Surface marking: about two finger-widths above the zygomatic arch, a thumb’s width behind the zygomatic bone.
The artery enters the skull through the foramen spinosum.
depth.check: OpenStax describes the artery of the foramen spinosum without naming it.

depth.t: Its branches groove the inner surface of the skull.
It is a branch of the maxillary artery.

clinical.t: A torn artery bleeds between the skull and the dura: an extradural haematoma. The patient may seem well at first, but the growing clot presses on the brain and can kill within hours, so it is a surgical emergency.
clinical.check: OpenStax says “a haematoma (collection of blood) between the brain and interior of the skull”; the term “extradural” needs an approved source.

trap.t: An extradural haematoma is usually arterial (middle meningeal artery); a subdural haematoma is usually venous (bridging veins).

cards.objective: Recognise the cribriform plate from its description.
cards.front: Name it: a small, flat, sieve-like part of the ethmoid bone in the roof of the nasal cavity, pierced by openings for olfactory nerve branches.

why.t: “Cribrum” means sieve: the plate is pierced by many small olfactory foramina. Nerve branches from the smell-sensing area of the nasal cavity pass up through them to enter the brain.

simpler.t: It is a thin plate full of tiny holes, like a sieve. The nerves for smell pass through the holes from the nose to the brain.

depth.t: Lies on either side of the crista galli, in the midline of the anterior cranial fossa.
Forms the narrow roof of the nasal cavity.
The crista galli gives anterior attachment to one of the coverings of the brain.
The anterior cranial fossa, which it helps to floor, holds the frontal lobes.

clinical.t: A fracture through the cribriform plate can tear the olfactory nerve fibres, causing loss of smell, and can let cerebrospinal fluid leak from the nose.
clinical.check: OpenStax confirms that head trauma can shear the olfactory axons and cause loss of smell (anosmia); a fracture of the cribriform plate and a leak of cerebrospinal fluid from the nose are not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–9, 12–16, 20).

trap.t: Do not mix up the cribriform plate (ethmoid bone, smell) with the optic canal (sphenoid bone, sight).

cards.objective: Identify the ethmoid bone on the skeleton.

why.t: A single midline bone between the orbits that forms the roof and upper walls of the nasal cavity (ethmoid bone). The nerve fibres for smell pass through its cribriform plate into the brain.

simpler.t: The ethmoid bone sits behind the top of your nose, between your eyes.

depth.t: Cribriform plates: flat plates either side of it (“sieve”), pierced by small olfactory foramina.
Perpendicular plate: forms the upper part of the nasal septum.
Superior and middle nasal conchae: thin curved plates projecting from each side wall of the nasal cavity.
Ethmoid air cells: many small air spaces with very thin walls, between the nasal cavity and the orbit.
Orbital surface: forms much of the medial wall of each orbit, with the lacrimal bone.

clinical.t: Blunt force to the face, as in a car accident. The olfactory nerve fibres are sheared where they pass through the cribriform plate. The frontal lobe moves relative to the ethmoid bone, tearing the fine fibres.

trap.t: The inferior nasal concha is a separate bone; only the superior and middle conchae belong to the ethmoid.

cards.objective: Identify the frontal bone on the skeleton.

why.t: The single bone of the forehead, which also forms the roof of each orbit (frontal bone). Inside the skull, it forms most of the floor of the anterior cranial fossa.

simpler.t: The frontal bone is your forehead bone.

depth.t: Glabella: a slight hollow between the eyebrows, at the front midline.
Supraorbital margin: the upper rim of each orbit.
Supraorbital foramen: an opening near the middle of each margin, for a sensory nerve to the forehead.
Brow ridges: rounded thickenings just above each margin, behind the eyebrows.
Orbital part: a flat region that forms the roof of the orbits and the floor of the anterior cranial fossa.

clinical.t: A cold or sinus congestion. The lining of the frontal sinus swells and blocks its narrow passage to the nasal cavity. The blocked sinus fills with fluid, and the pressure causes pain.

trap.t: The frontal bone forms the roof of the orbit; the floor is mainly the maxilla.

cards.objective: Identify the hyoid bone on the skeleton.

why.t: A small U-shaped bone in the upper neck that touches no other bone (hyoid bone). It is the base of the tongue, and it moves when you swallow and speak.

simpler.t: The hyoid is a small U-shaped bone in your neck, below your jaw.

depth.t: U shape: a small curved bone, open at the back.
Body: the front of the U.
Tips: the two ends of the U, pointing backwards.
Muscle attachments: small muscles attach to it from above and from below.
Ligament attachment: a ligament from the styloid process of the temporal bone supports it.

clinical.t: Strong pressure on the front of the neck, as in strangulation. The hyoid bone may break. The hyoid moves with the tongue, larynx and pharynx in swallowing and speaking.
clinical.check: A fracture of the hyoid is not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–9, 12–16, 20); its role in swallowing and speech is.

trap.t: The hyoid is not a skull bone: it touches no other bone at all.

cards.objective: Identify the inferior nasal concha on the skeleton.

why.t: A curved plate of bone projecting into the nasal cavity from its lower side wall (inferior nasal concha). Unlike the other two conchae, it is a separate bone, not part of the ethmoid.

simpler.t: The inferior nasal concha is a curved shelf of bone inside your nose.

depth.t: Curved plate: curves downwards as it projects into the nasal cavity.
Size: the largest of the three nasal conchae.
Attached edge: fixed to the lower part of the side wall of the nasal cavity.
Visible from the front: it can easily be seen looking into the front opening of the nasal cavity.

clinical.t: Heavy crying. Nothing is damaged: the tear drain behind the inferior concha is overloaded. Extra tears entering the nasal cavity behind the concha also drain forwards.

trap.t: The inferior concha is a separate bone, unlike the superior and middle conchae of the ethmoid.

cards.objective: Identify the lacrimal bone on the skeleton.

why.t: A small rectangular bone at the front of the inner wall of the orbit (lacrimal bone). Tears drain from the eye through a canal beside it into the nose.

simpler.t: The lacrimal bone is a tiny bone at the inner corner of your eye socket.

depth.t: Shape: a small, rectangular plate of bone.
Lacrimal fossa: a shallow hollow in its front part.
Nasolacrimal canal: runs down from the fossa towards the nasal cavity.
Orbital surface: forms the front of the medial wall of the orbit.

clinical.t: Crying, or an irritated eye, increases the flow of tears. Nothing is damaged: the tear drain is working, but overloaded. Tears normally drain backwards in the nasal cavity; extra fluid also drains forwards.

trap.t: The nasolacrimal duct opens into the nasal cavity, behind the inferior concha, not into the mouth.

cards.objective: Identify the mandible on the skeleton.

why.t: The lower jaw: the only skull bone that moves (mandible). It is one of two unpaired facial bones; the other is the vomer.

simpler.t: The mandible is your lower jaw bone.

depth.t: Body: the horizontal, U-shaped part that holds the lower teeth.
Ramus: the upright part at the back of each side (“ramus” means branch).
Angle: the corner where the body and ramus meet.
Alveolar process: the top edge of the body, which anchors the lower teeth.

clinical.t: Opening the mouth too wide, as in a large bite, or a blow to the jaw. The jaw joint dislocates: the condyle moves in front of the articular tubercle. The condyle is stuck in front of the tubercle and cannot slide back.

trap.t: The condyle forms the jaw joint; the coronoid process is the front projection, for a biting muscle.

cards.objective: Identify the maxilla on the skeleton.

why.t: One of two bones forming the upper jaw, most of the hard palate and part of the orbit floor (maxilla). It contains the largest paranasal sinus, the maxillary sinus, just below the orbit.

simpler.t: The maxilla is your upper jaw bone.

depth.t: Alveolar process: the curved lower edge that holds the upper teeth.
Palatine process: a shelf that meets its partner to form the front three-quarters of the hard palate.
Orbital surface: forms most of the inner floor of the orbit.
Maxillary sinus: the largest paranasal sinus, below the orbit.

clinical.t: A sinus infection, often after a cold. It affects the maxillary sinus, the sinus most often infected. The sinus opens into the nasal cavity high on its inner wall, so it drains poorly.

trap.t: The maxillae form the front three-quarters of the hard palate; the palatine bones form the back quarter.

cards.objective: Identify the nasal bone on the skeleton.

why.t: One of two small bones that form the bridge of the nose (nasal bone). They also support the cartilages that form the sides of the nose.

simpler.t: The nasal bones form the hard top of your nose.

depth.t: Midline joint: the two bones meet each other in the midline.
Bridge of the nose: together they form its bony base.
Lower edges: support the cartilages of the side walls of the nose.
Upper and side edges: meet the frontal bone above and the maxillae at the sides.

clinical.t: A blow to the nose. The nasal bones break: these are the bones damaged when the nose is broken. The thin bones form the bony bridge, so a blow drives them sideways or inwards.
clinical.check: OpenStax says these bones break in a broken nose; displacement of the bridge is not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–9, 12–16, 20).

trap.t: The nasal bones form only the bridge of the nose; cartilage, missing from the dry skull, shapes the rest.

cards.objective: Identify the occipital bone on the skeleton.

why.t: The single bone of the back and base of the skull, around the foramen magnum (occipital bone). Its condyles rest on the first cervical vertebra, so the skull sits on the vertebral column.

simpler.t: The occipital bone is the bone at the back of your head.

depth.t: External occipital protuberance: a small bump at the back midline, where a ligament of the neck attaches.
Superior nuchal lines: lines either side of the bump: the highest point where neck muscles attach.
Foramen magnum: the large opening (“great aperture”) in the base, for the spinal cord.
Hypoglossal canals: openings at the front edge of the foramen magnum, for a nerve to the tongue.
Venous grooves: large curved grooves on the inner wall, ending at the jugular foramen.

clinical.t: A blow to the front or side of the head. The base of the occipital bone may break on the opposite side (contrecoup), a basilar fracture. In a contrecoup fracture, the bone breaks opposite the point of impact.

trap.t: The occipital condyles meet the first cervical vertebra (atlas), not the second (axis).

cards.objective: Name the ossicle at the oval window.
cards.front: Which auditory ossicle is attached to the oval window?

why.t: The stapes is attached to the inner ear, at the oval window of the cochlea. Vibrations passing through the oval window set the fluid of the cochlea moving in waves.

simpler.t: The ossicles are three tiny bones in your ear that pass sound inwards.

depth.t: Malleus: “Hammer”: attached to the eardrum, and joined to the incus.
Incus: “Anvil”: between the other two, joined to both.
Stapes: “Stirrup”: joined to the incus, and attached to the inner ear at the oval window.
A chain of joints: the three are joined end to end, from the eardrum to the inner ear.
Footplate of the stapes: its flat base fills the oval window.

clinical.t: Abnormal bone growth fixes the stapes in the oval window (otosclerosis). The stapes must move to send vibrations through the oval window.
clinical.check: Otosclerosis is not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–9, 12–16, 20); the role of the oval window is.

trap.t: The malleus is attached to the eardrum; it is the stapes that meets the oval window.

cards.source: OpenStax A&P 2e: 14.1 Sensory Perception; 7.2 The Skull

cards.objective: Identify the palatine bone on the skeleton.

why.t: One of a pair of irregular bones that form the back quarter of the hard palate (palatine bone). They also form small parts of the side walls of the nasal cavity and of the orbit.

simpler.t: The palatine bones form the back of the bony roof of your mouth.

depth.t: Horizontal plate: its largest region; with its partner it forms the back quarter of the hard palate.
Nasal part: adds small areas to the side walls of the nasal cavity.
Orbital part: a small contribution to the orbit.
Shape: an irregular bone, paired with its partner.

clinical.t: The two halves of the hard palate fail to fuse during development (cleft palate). The palatine plates and palatine processes leave a gap in the midline. The gap connects the mouth and nasal cavity, so no seal forms.

trap.t: The palatine bones form only the back quarter of the hard palate.

cards.objective: Identify the parietal bone on the skeleton.

why.t: One of a pair of curved bones forming most of the upper sides and top of the skull (parietal bone). The two parietal bones meet along the top of the skull at the sagittal suture.

simpler.t: The parietal bones form the top and sides of your head.

depth.t: Sagittal border: meets the other parietal bone at the sagittal suture.
Frontal border: meets the frontal bone at the coronal suture.
Occipital border: meets the occipital bone at the lambdoid suture.
Squamous border: meets the squamous part of the temporal bone at the squamous suture.

clinical.t: The sagittal suture closes too early (craniosynostosis). The joint between the two parietal bones fuses. Growth is diverted to the sides of the skull, which grow upwards.

trap.t: The sagittal suture joins the two parietal bones; the coronal suture joins them to the frontal bone.

cards.objective: Identify the temporal bone on the skeleton.

why.t: The bone of the lower side of the skull, around the ear (temporal bone). Its petrous part houses the middle and inner ear.

simpler.t: The temporal bone is the skull bone around your ear.

depth.t: Squamous part: the flattened upper part.
Zygomatic process: projects forwards to form the back of the zygomatic arch.
Mastoid process: a large bump behind the earlobe, where muscles attach.
Petrous part: a dense diagonal ridge inside the skull, holding the middle and inner ear.
Mandibular fossa and articular tubercle: a hollow and a ridge in front of the ear canal, for the jaw joint.

clinical.t: A blow that fractures the base of the skull (basilar fracture). It affects the internal carotid artery, in the carotid canal of the temporal bone. The internal carotid is one of the two main arteries supplying the brain.

trap.t: The mastoid process is the bump behind the ear; the styloid process is a separate, pen-like spike.

cards.objective: Identify the vomer on the skeleton.

why.t: A single, triangular bone that forms the lower and back part of the nasal septum (vomer). Seen from behind, it forms the whole height of the nasal septum.

simpler.t: The vomer is a bone in the middle of your nose, at the lower back.

depth.t: Triangular shape: a flat, triangular plate in the midline.
Upper edge: lies below the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid.
Front edge: the septal cartilage fills the gap between it and the perpendicular plate.
Back edge: divides the two back openings of the nasal cavity.

clinical.t: A septum bent to one side, from development or an injury. It affects the bony and cartilage parts of the septum, including the vomer. The septum divides the nasal cavity, so bending it narrows one side.
clinical.check: A deviated septum is not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–9, 12–16, 20); the septum’s role is.

trap.t: The vomer forms the lower and back septum; the ethmoid’s perpendicular plate forms the upper part.

cards.objective: Identify the zygomatic bone on the skeleton.

why.t: The cheekbone, which forms much of the outer wall of the orbit (zygomatic bone). Its temporal process forms the front of the zygomatic arch.

simpler.t: The zygomatic bone is your cheekbone.

depth.t: Orbital part: forms much of the lateral wall and the lateral floor of the orbit.
Orbital margin: the outer and lower rim of the front opening of the orbit.
Temporal process: a short projection backwards, forming the front of the zygomatic arch.
Upward part: rises at the outer edge of the orbit; a landmark for finding the pterion.

clinical.t: A blow to the side of the head, just behind the upward part of the zygomatic bone. It affects the pterion, with a major artery to the brain’s coverings just inside it. The pterion is the weakest part of the skull, and bleeding there presses on the brain.

trap.t: The zygomatic arch has two parts: the front from the zygomatic bone, the back from the temporal bone.
